findings.title: 22 exported components have no permission guard
findings.detail: {'activity': 14, 'activity-alias': 2, 'service': 1, 'receiver': 5} of the app's 267 components are reachable by any installed application (exported=true and no android:permission). Examples: SplashScreenActivityV2, SplashScreenGooglePaymentActivity, VerificationByVNeIDActivity, QRReceiverActivity, IdentityCardCaptureActivity, CustomTabActivity. For a wallet this is the classic intent-redirection / confused-deputy surface: a malicious app can start these with attacker-controlled extras and URIs.
findings.recommendation: Guard every exported entry point with a signature-level permission, validate all incoming extras/URIs against an allowlist, and re-check the caller uid for value-moving flows.

findings.title: 21 deep links resolve into exported activities
findings.detail: App-link domains: https://go.zalopay.vn, https://km.zalopay.vn, https://kmzalopay.onelink.me, https://onelink.zalopay.vn. 16 use a non-http scheme, which any app can claim, so link parameters arrive from an untrusted source. Auto-verify protects only the https hosts.
findings.recommendation: Treat every deep-link parameter as untrusted input, sign/validate hand-off tokens, and require re-authentication before any transaction is pre-filled from a link.

findings.title: WebView.addJavascriptInterface used at 13 call sites
findings.detail: A JavaScript bridge object is injected into a WebView. On API < 17 every public method was reachable from JS; on modern Android only @JavascriptInterface methods are, but any URL loaded in that WebView inherits access to those methods - the textbook route for a cross-app bridge if a URL can be influenced by an attacker.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the bridge to the minimal method set, validate the origin of every load, and never mix the bridge WebView with untrusted content.

findings.title: 49 permissions requested, 13 dangerous across 9 groups
findings.detail: Runtime-sensitive groups: NOTIFICATIONS(1), CONTACTS(2), PHONE(1), STORAGE(2), LOCATION(2), CALENDAR(2), MICROPHONE(1), CAMERA(1), MEDIA(1). Custom/OEM permissions: 15. Each dangerous permission is a user-visible data channel that must be justified at runtime and in the Play listing.
findings.recommendation: Apply just-in-time requests, keep a machine-readable permission-to-feature map, and ship a privacy manifest that ties each SDK to the data it can collect.
evidence: dangerous: POST_NOTIFICATIONS, READ_CONTACTS, READ_PHONE_STATE, WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, WRITE_CALENDAR, READ_CALENDAR, RECORD_AUDIO, CAMERA, WRITE_CONTACTS, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO

findings.title: Dynamic class loading observed (6 call sites)
findings.detail: DexClassLoader/PathClassLoader/InMemoryDexClassLoader references mean bytecode can enter the process outside the APK. For a payments app this is legitimate only for signed plugin modules, and it must be integrity-checked before load.
findings.recommendation: Verify a signature over every downloaded dex/jar, load from app-private storage only, and prefer the platform's split/feature delivery.

findings.title: No declarative certificate pinning in the network security config
findings.detail: res/xml/network_security_config.xml declares 1 domain-config (e.g. storage.googleapis.com) and no <pin-set>. Any pinning therefore lives in application code (OkHttp CertificatePinner / trust manager), which is invisible to the platform and to third-party SDKs that open their own connections.
findings.recommendation: Publish pins in the NSC so every consumer of the process-wide TLS stack benefits, with a backup pin and a rotation expiry.

findings.title: QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES broadens app-visibility beyond the <queries> list
findings.detail: The manifest both declares <queries> (27 entries) and requests QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, which Google Play restricts to specific use cases. Combined with the PackageManager calls observed in DEX, the app can enumerate installed apps (fraud/risk signals, but also fingerprinting).
findings.recommendation: Drop QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES and rely on the explicit <queries> allowlist where possible.
evidence: <queries>: com.vnid, com.zing.zalo, com.facebook.katana, com.google.android.apps.maps, com.instagram.android, com.facebook.lite, com.samsung.android.mapsagent, com.xiaomi.mipicks, intent:android.intent.action.VIEW, intent:android.media.action.IMAGE_CAPTURE

findings.title: Signing key is self-signed with a 25-year validity window
findings.detail: Subject CN=Vu Manh Hieu / issuer CN=Vu Manh Hieu, rsaEncryption 2048 bit, valid Apr 21 15:41:14 2016 GMT -> Apr 15 15:41:14 2041 GMT, SHA-256 59dd31fdf36070a0d7f8c8cde843fac371df7f1a915c0136c9c9b55992e8cdae. Android does not check expiry for APK verification, but a single long-lived key with no rotation lineage means key compromise is unrecoverable for existing installs.
findings.recommendation: Use Play App Signing with a rotating upload key, and publish a v3 proof-of-rotation lineage so future keys are auditable.

findings.title: Production build flags are clean (not debuggable, backup disabled)
findings.detail: android:debuggable is absent, allowBackup=false, dataExtractionRules=@7F160004. A debuggable release would allow JDWP attach and arbitrary file pulls via run-as.
findings.recommendation: Keep these as release-only properties and assert them in CI (e.g. a bundle-lint gate).

findings.title: Signature scheme: v2+v3 on every module, v1 only on bundletool splits
findings.detail: All five modules carry a v2 (0x7109871a) and v3 (0xf05368c0) block, so the whole-file digest covers the base APK. META-INF/BNDLTOOL.RSA (a v1 JAR signature) is present in 4 configuration splits only - a bundletool artefact, not a build setting. v1 is dead weight under minSdk=26 and is also the surface of the classic Janus/strip attacks.
findings.recommendation: No action required; consider v4/fs-verity sidecars for incremental install.

findings.title: Native libraries are toolchain-hardened (mean 5.07/6)
findings.detail: 28 shared objects: PIE=27/28, NX=27/28, RELRO=23/28, full-RELRO=23/28, canary=25/28.
findings.recommendation: Keep -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now,-z,noexecstack and fstack-protector-strong in the NDK build.

findings.title: All 9 ContentProviders are non-exported
findings.detail: Every declared authority (FileProvider, Firebase, Facebook init provider, WorkManager, etc.) is exported=false; the file-sharing surface is therefore limited to explicit grantUriPermissions flows.
findings.recommendation: No action.

findings.title: No base-config cleartext exemption (platform default: cleartext blocked)
findings.detail: cleartextTrafficPermitted is not set at base-config level; because targetSdk=36 the platform default denies cleartext for all domains not explicitly listed.
findings.recommendation: No action; keep the allowlist empty.

findings.title: App-layer pinning present (12 OkHttp sites, 0 SHA-256 pin digests in the string pool)
findings.detail: CertificatePinner / pin digests live in application code, so HTTPS trust is additionally constrained for the OkHttp stack used by first-party calls. Because the pins are not in the platform NSC, SDKs with their own HTTP stacks bypass them entirely.
findings.recommendation: Document a rotation window, keep a backup pin, and cover every host that carries session or payment data - including mini-program and bank-app hand-off hosts.

findings.title: Device/app integrity and anti-tamper signals present
findings.detail: String and symbol evidence for: play_integrity(48), root_detection(248), hook_detection(8), emulator_detection(2), biometric_gate(101), certificate_pinning(14), code_obfuscation(9), screenshot_or_hook_strings(7). Combined with screenshot protection (FLAG_SECURE) and biometric gating of the payment flow, the app implements a layered client-side risk posture.
findings.recommendation: Treat client-side signals as *risk inputs* only; the server must remain the authority for every value-moving decision.

findings.title: 26 on-device ML models shipped (12371 KiB)
findings.detail: TensorFlow-Lite / ncnn artefacts plus ML Kit bundled models run inference locally (OCR, barcode, face, liveness). Keeping inference on-device reduces the amount of biometric or document imagery leaving the handset.
findings.recommendation: Keep model updates signed, and document the inference boundary in the privacy notice.

findings.title: APK carries a Play source stamp (distribution provenance)
findings.detail: The APK Signing Block contains id 0x6dff800d (source stamp), together with the 0x42726577 'Brew' and 0x204b5041 'APK ' padding blocks. These are written by Play App Signing, so the artifact is a Play-signed build re-packaged by APKPure, not a rebuild from source.
findings.recommendation: Treat the APK as authentic-for-distribution but verify the distribution channel.

findings.title: Unattributed namespaces remain after vendor matching
findings.detail: 40 namespaces could not be mapped to a known vendor. The largest is <default> (12 classes) - random-looking identifiers that suggest either a rebranded SDK or R8 repackaging of a first-party module.
findings.recommendation: Maintain an internal namespace allowlist so every shipped package is attributable to a team.

findings.title: Split-APK packaging: base + ABI/locale/density configuration splits
findings.detail: 6464 entries across 5 APKs (config.armeabi_v7a=32, config.en=6, config.vi=6, config.xhdpi=258, base=6162). Splits must be signature-identical to the base module or the installer rejects them.
findings.recommendation: Verify split signatures in CI (apksigner verify on every module).

findings.title: 3 trust/config artefacts inside assets/
findings.detail: Bundled key material is public by definition (anything in the APK can be read). These files are only meaningful as pins/verification keys, never as secrets.
findings.recommendation: Audit that no long-term secret is packaged; rotate anything that was.

findings.title: 141 version-stamped third-party libraries from 62 groups
findings.detail: META-INF/*.version files give an exact, build-time SBOM. Third-party code is ~99% of the class space, so the app's real attack surface is mostly the SDKs' surface.
findings.recommendation: Feed these stamps into an SCA pipeline (OSV/CVE matching) and fail the build on known vulnerable versions.
